**Check claims against evidence one at a time.** An intrinsic hallucination contradicts the supplied source. An extrinsic hallucination adds something the source does not support, even if it might be true elsewhere. A single response can contain both supported and unsupported claims. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685)

If a source says revenue was 10 million, “revenue was 20 million” contradicts it for the same period. “Profit was 2 million” is unsupported if the source says nothing about profit. Treating both as generic semantic mismatch loses a useful distinction.

Split the answer into atomic claims, retrieve relevant evidence windows, and classify support, contradiction, or insufficient evidence. Dates, negation, arithmetic, and entity alignment need explicit checks because broad text similarity can miss them.

**Latency needs a measured budget.** A small NLI model, batching, and cached evidence can help, but a universal sub-20 ms promise is unjustified without hardware and workload assumptions. Measure end-to-end p99 and error rates. When evidence is missing, abstain or retrieve more rather than interpreting absence of contradiction as support.

**Technical details and references.**

An intrinsic hallucination contradicts the supplied evidence; an extrinsic one adds a claim not supported by it, even if that claim happens to be true elsewhere. Split the response into atomic claims, retrieve each claim's evidence, and use entailment/contradiction scoring with an explicit unsupported category. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685)

For example, a passage reporting revenue of 10 million does not support a claim about profit, and contradicts revenue of 20 million for the same period. Negation, dates, arithmetic, and incomplete context need dedicated checks. A compact NLI model, batching, caching, and short evidence windows can reduce latency, but “under 20 ms” depends on hardware and workload. Measure end-to-end tail latency and calibrated error rates; abstain when evidence is insufficient.
